main_damage_causes: Removal of both the Christmas garden confrontation and the post-funeral confrontation eliminates the entire adversarial arc between Harry and Scrimgeour across Half-Blood Prince, leaving the Deathly Hallows will scene without dramatic or moral context

The will scene itself is significantly defanged: the wand-jabbing confrontation, the 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange, the Snitch-test deduction, and the scar display are all absent, replacing a dangerous and morally complex antagonist with a weary, semi-sympathetic official

Scrimgeour's posthumous redemption (his refusal to betray Harry under torture) loses its retroactive impact because the film never established him as a fully flawed but formidable antagonist — the moral surprise of his death is diminished

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Sitting Room - Will reading): Scrimgeour skips interrogation about Snitch's flesh memory / open-it-yourself test
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 182-198: Scrimgeour conducts a prolonged, shrewd interrogation about why Dumbledore left the Snitch, correctly deduces it may open only for Harry, and deliberately places it in Harry's palm to test whether it opens — demonstrating his intelligence, tenacity, and investigative instincts as a former Head of the Auror office.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Scrimgeour simply places the Snitch in Harry's palm as part of reading the will, with no deduction, no test, no line of interrogation about flesh memory, and no attempt to force it open. The moment passes without drama on Scrimgeour's part.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This removes one of Scrimgeour's defining book moments: a display of sharp Auror-trained intelligence. His ability to deduce the Snitch's enchantment and engineer a test shows he is a genuine threat and a formidable opponent — not merely an obstructive bureaucrat. Losing this collapses his characterization from 'dangerous, clever old lion' to 'officious delivery man.' It also transfers the flesh-memory insight to Hermione (Film Scene 5), further diminishing Scrimgeour's agency.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Drawing Room): Hermione explains flesh memory / Snitch enchantment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 189-192: It is Scrimgeour himself who explains the flesh-memory enchantment of Snitches and deduces that Dumbledore may have hidden something inside it — this is a showcase of his Auror expertise and investigative cunning.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5: Hermione explains the flesh-memory property of Snitches to Harry after the fact, effectively taking on the insight that was Scrimgeour's in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: By transferring Scrimgeour's deduction to Hermione, the film strips him of a key demonstration of competence. The book uses this moment to show why the Wizarding world trusts Scrimgeour: he is sharp, experienced, and dangerous. Giving it to Hermione in a later scene severs it entirely from Scrimgeour's characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Sitting Room): Sword of Gryffindor confrontation is defused; no wand-jabbing or loss of temper
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 210-222: The argument over the sword escalates dramatically — Scrimgeour loses his temper, jabs Harry hard in the chest with his wand (singeing his T-shirt), shouts 'You go too far!', and physically advances on Harry. This eruption reveals the controlled menace beneath his political surface and gives Harry his second 'I must not tell lies' scar-raising moment, echoing his defiance of Umbridge.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Scrimgeour states the sword is missing, tells Harry he is 'not your enemy,' looks haunted, and exits quietly. There is no escalation, no physical threat, no loss of temper, no scar display, no 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's confrontation is essential: it shows Scrimgeour's barely-suppressed authoritarian ruthlessness cracking through his polished exterior. The wand-jab is a physical act of intimidation by a sitting Minister against a seventeen-year-old, which crystallizes the Ministry's moral bankruptcy. Removing it makes Scrimgeour seem weary and almost sympathetic rather than dangerous and self-serving. The thematic payoff — Harry raising his Umbridge scar for the second time — is also lost entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Sitting Room): 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 85-86 and 113-114: In both the Christmas confrontation and the post-funeral confrontation, Scrimgeour's verdict — 'Dumbledore's man through and through, aren't you, Potter?' — and Harry's proud, defiant 'Yeah, I am. Glad we straightened that out' / 'That's right' is a defining thematic statement. It encapsulates Harry's allegiance and his rejection of the Ministry's authority, and it is repeated at the funeral for resonance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Neither the phrase nor its sentiment is spoken. Harry's defiant self-definition as Dumbledore's man is absent from the will scene. There is no equivalent exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This line is one of the most thematically charged in Harry's arc across Half-Blood Prince and Deathly Hallows — it defines his moral identity and his refusal to be co-opted by institutional authority. Its absence from the film removes a key moment of character definition and weakens the thematic throughline about loyalty to Dumbledore versus loyalty to the Ministry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Sitting Room): Scrimgeour's interrogation techniques softened; no challenge to the trio being 'together'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 141-143: Scrimgeour opens by demanding to speak to them individually, and when Harry refuses, Scrimgeour gives 'Harry a cold, appraising look,' calculating whether 'it was worthwhile opening hostilities this early.' This cat-and-mouse power dynamic establishes him as a seasoned interrogator.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Scrimgeour simply proceeds with the group immediately, with no attempt to separate them, no cold appraisal, and no sense of calculated concession. The adversarial tension is absent from the outset.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but meaningful loss: the book's opening gambit reveals Scrimgeour's instinct to divide and interrogate — classic Auror tradecraft. Removing it softens him from the first moment of the scene, reducing the sense that Harry and company are being professionally interrogated by a dangerous official.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Sitting Room): Scrimgeour's haunted, sympathetic exit ('I came alone. I don't really need them anymore')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 222: Scrimgeour's exit after the will scene is cold and hard — 'His expression hardened. He turned away without another word and limped from the room.' There is no moment of vulnerability or pathos; he leaves as an adversary, defeated but not humanized.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Scrimgeour says 'I came alone. I don't really need them anymore...' while gazing out the window with 'haunted' eyes, implying he knows he is a marked man and is already half-broken. He exits with a quality of tragic dignity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This invented beat prematurely humanizes Scrimgeour in a way the book never does during a living scene. In the books, his heroism is revealed only posthumously through Lupin's report of his torture and refusal to betray Harry (Book Scene 232-233). Making him visibly mournful and self-aware before his death shifts him from 'flawed antagonist redeemed by his death' to 'tragic hero who knew his fate' — a different, softer character. It undercuts the retroactive moral surprise of his death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1-2 (Daily Prophet / Ministry Atrium): Scrimgeour's introduction is a public address, not the Prime Minister meeting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 5-15: Scrimgeour's introduction is an intimate, private scene with the Muggle Prime Minister in which his physical presence ('like an old lion'), his brisk authority, his political maneuvering over Kingsley and Herbert Chorley, and his decisive manner are all established in close detail. It is one of the most characterizing passages in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scenes 1-2: Scrimgeour is introduced only as a photograph/newsreel in the Daily Prophet giving a public speech in the Ministry Atrium. No private interaction, no physical intimidation, no dry wit ('That's because he's a wizard'), no establishing of his relationship with the Muggle world.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Prime Minister scene is the fullest characterization of Scrimgeour in the entire book corpus: his lion-like appearance, his shrewdness, his barely-disguised contempt for Muggle authority, his political ruthlessness, and his black humor are all on display. Replacing it with a propaganda-speech photograph removes the intimate portrait entirely and replaces it with an image of him as a generic wartime official. Audiences never see who he is before they see him as an obstacle to Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film: Christmas garden confrontation (Half-Blood Prince book material) entirely absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 43-88: The Christmas confrontation at the Burrow is a full scene in which Scrimgeour manipulates Percy's family reunion as a pretext, corners Harry alone in the garden, attempts to recruit him as a 'mascot,' is rebuffed with increasing force, asks about Dumbledore's movements, and is told 'Dumbledore's man through and through.' This establishes the full adversarial dynamic between Harry and Scrimgeour before Deathly Hallows.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus. The will scene in Deathly Hallows Part 1 (Film Scene 4) is the only substantial Scrimgeour-Harry interaction present in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Christmas scene is the foundation of the Harry-Scrimgeour relationship. Without it, the antagonism in the will scene arrives without context; the audience has no basis for Harry's contempt, no knowledge that Scrimgeour already tried to use him once, no awareness of Stan Shunpike as the emblem of Ministry injustice, and no prior establishment of the 'Dumbledore's man' theme. The relationship is structurally hollowed out.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film: Post-funeral confrontation (Half-Blood Prince book material) entirely absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 108-116: After Dumbledore's funeral, Scrimgeour again approaches Harry, attempts to extract information about where Dumbledore went and what they were doing, offers Auror protection (which Harry dismisses), and is again rebuffed with the repeated 'Dumbledore's man through and through.' This is the final confrontation of the HBP arc and the culmination of their antagonistic dynamic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene closes the arc of Scrimgeour as Harry's antagonist in HBP and thematically prepares the ground for Scrimgeour's death and posthumous redemption in DH. Without it, the arc has no conclusion — Scrimgeour simply disappears between films without a final defining confrontation, making his death feel like the removal of a background functionary rather than a morally complex figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4: Stan Shunpike injustice not raised by Harry; no moral indictment of Ministry's wrongful imprisonment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 40-41, 70-73: Stan Shunpike's unjust imprisonment is Harry's primary moral weapon against Scrimgeour — he deploys it twice, at Christmas and at the funeral, as the concrete proof that the Ministry cares more about appearances than justice. 'You're making Stan a scapegoat, just like you want to make me a mascot.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Stan Shunpike is never mentioned. The moral critique of the Ministry's abuses is absent from Harry's confrontation with Scrimgeour.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Stan Shunpike's case is the book's specific, tangible example of Ministry injustice — it grounds the political critique in a human victim and gives Harry's opposition to Scrimgeour moral weight beyond mere personal pride. Without it, Harry's antagonism seems more like adolescent defiance than principled resistance. The film's Scrimgeour is critiqued more vaguely, losing the thematic sharpness.
